q: What is the main difference between the chapter's two kinds of loop?
options: A condition loop runs its block once, a counted loop runs it twice
A counted loop works only on text, a condition loop only on numbers
A condition loop repeats while an expression is true, a counted loop runs once per item of a sequence
A condition loop always stops after ten passes, a counted loop never stops
why: Some loops repeat while a condition holds, others run once for each item of a sequence.

q: Why can you not always tell in advance how many times a condition loop will run?
options: Python picks the number of passes at random each time
It stops when its expression turns false, which depends on the data the program meets
A condition loop always runs at least one hundred passes
The block of such a loop is not allowed to change any variable
why: A condition loop repeats as long as an expression is true, so its length depends on the data rather than on a count.

q: What does this program print?
why: The loop keeps going while n is not 1, so the number of passes depends on the data: 6, 3, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 takes eight steps.

q: How does a while statement differ from an if statement with the same condition?
options: The block of a while statement can never contain an if statement
After the block, execution jumps back and the condition is tested again
A while statement tests its condition only once, before the first pass
An if statement repeats its block, a while statement runs it once
why: Unlike an if statement, a while statement jumps back to the start of its block and tests the condition again after every pass.

q: What does this program print?
code:
total = 0
n = 1
while total < 10:
    total += n
    n += 1
print(total, n)
why: The condition is tested after every pass: total goes 1, 3, 6, 10 and the loop stops as soon as total is no longer below 10, with n having been raised to 5.

q: Which of these can end a deliberate while True: loop?
options: Only break, since nothing else can leave the loop
break, return, sys.exit() or an exception
The condition becoming false after enough passes
Python stops it by itself after about a thousand passes
why: A loop whose condition never becomes false runs until something inside it leaves: break, return, sys.exit() or an exception.

q: What does this program print?
why: while True: never ends by its condition, so only the break inside leaves the loop, and it fires on the first pass where n exceeds 10, which is n = 12.

q: A loop starts with while count < 5: and its block prints count but never changes it. What is the problem?
options: Python refuses to run a while loop whose block has no assignment
The condition can never become false, so nothing inside ever leaves the loop
The loop runs exactly five times because the limit is 5
The loop runs zero times, because count is not compared with anything
why: If the condition never becomes false the program keeps going forever, unless something inside leaves the loop.

q: Why is the length of a counted loop known before it starts?
options: Python counts the passes of the last run and repeats that number
The programmer must always write the number of passes inside the block
It stops when an expression turns false, so the count is fixed by the data
It runs once for each item of a sequence that already exists
why: A counted loop runs its block once for each item of a sequence, so its length is known before it starts.

q: What does this program print?
code:
words = ['a', 'bb', 'ccc']
count = 0
for w in words:
    count += len(w)
print(count)
options: abccc
why: The loop takes each of the three words in turn and adds its length, 1 + 2 + 3.

q: What does a for statement do with the iterable it is given?
options: Takes each item in turn, assigns it to its variable and runs the block once for each
Copies the whole iterable into the variable and runs the block once
Runs the block once and then tests a condition again
Sorts the items first and then runs the block on the largest
why: A for statement takes each item of an iterable in turn, assigns it to its variable and runs the block once for each.

q: What does this program print?
code:
total = 0
for i in range(1, 5):
    total += i * i
print(total)
why: range(1, 5) gives 1, 2, 3, 4 and the block adds their squares: 1 + 4 + 9 + 16.

q: What is range() for in the chapter's loops?
options: It repeats a block a fixed number of times without any loop
It converts a list of numbers into text
It checks whether a number lies between two limits
It makes a sequence of integers for a loop to go through
why: Loops need something to iterate over, and range() is the chapter's way of making a sequence of integers.

q: How many arguments can the range function take?
options: Exactly one, the stop value
Exactly two, start and stop
One, two or three
Any number, which it adds up
why: The range function makes an arithmetic progression of integers and takes one, two or three arguments.

q: Why does list(range(5)) not contain 5?
options: The counting starts at 0 and stops before the argument
range(5) starts at 1, so it holds 1 to 4
The last value is dropped whenever the list is printed
Python leaves out the value that equals the argument to save one step
why: With one argument range starts at 0 and the end point is never part of the sequence.

q: What does this program print?
code: print(len(range(7)), max(range(7)), sum(range(4)))
why: range(7) holds seven values 0 to 6, so its length is 7 and its largest value 6; range(4) holds 0, 1, 2, 3 which add up to 6.

q: A student wants the numbers 1 to 10 and writes range(1, 10). What is wrong?
options: The stop value is excluded, so it ends at 9 and range(1, 11) is needed
Nothing, because range includes both ends
It starts at 0 instead of 1
It gives ten numbers but in descending order
why: The end point of range is never part of the sequence, so range(1, 10) stops at 9.

q: Which call gives the same values as range(10)?
options: range(1, 10)
range(1, 11)
range(0, 9)
why: range(10), range(0, 10) and range(0, 10, 1) all give the same values, from 0 up to but not including 10.

q: What does this program print?
code: print(list(range(2, 6)) == list(range(2, 6, 1)), len(range(12, 16)), list(range(4, 4)))
options: True 5 []
False 4 []
True 4 []
True 4 [4]
why: The default step is 1, so both lists match; range(12, 16) holds 12 to 15, four values; and range(4, 4) begins where it must stop, so it is empty.

q: What does the third argument of range() do?
options: It sets how many values the range holds in total
It sets the value where the range stops
It sets the gap between one value and the next
It repeats every value that many times
why: A third argument is the step between values.

q: What does this program print?
code: print(list(range(1, 10, 3)), list(range(0, 10, 5)))
why: Each value is the previous plus the step, and the stop value is never reached or included: 10 and 10 are excluded.

q: Why does list(range(5, -1, -1)) end with 0 rather than -1?
options: The stop value is still excluded, even when counting down
The negative step turns -1 into 0
Python never produces negative numbers in a range
The stop value is included only when the step is negative
why: A negative step counts down, and the stop value is still excluded.

q: What does this program print?
code: print(list(range(10, 0, -3)), list(range(3, 5, -1)))
why: Counting down by 3 from 10 gives 10, 7, 4, 1 and the next value would pass the stop 0; range(3, 5, -1) starts below its stop while going down, so it is empty.

q: Why does range(1000000) not use much memory?
options: It keeps only the first ten values and guesses the rest
Python compresses the numbers into a text string
It is a list, but a list of small numbers takes little space
It produces its values when iterated instead of holding them in a list
why: A range is an object that produces its values when iterated, not a list holding them, which saves space.

q: What does this program print?
code:
r = range(3)
print(r, list(r), type(r).__name__)
options: range(0, 3) [0, 1, 2] range
range(3) [0, 1, 2] range
range(0, 3) range(0, 3) range
why: Printing a range shows range(0, 3), not the numbers; the numbers appear only when it is iterated, for example by list(), and its type is range.

q: Which job does each of enumerate and zip take over from index arithmetic?
options: enumerate walks several sequences together, zip adds a running count
Both add a count, but zip counts from the end
enumerate sorts the items, zip joins them into one string
enumerate adds a running count to the items, zip walks several sequences together
why: Two built-in functions replace most index arithmetic: one adds a count, the other walks several sequences together.

q: Why is enumerate preferred to range(len(a)) when both the position and the item are needed?
options: It is the only way Python allows to read a list item
It runs faster because it skips the first item
It hands out the position and the item together, with no index arithmetic
It returns only the positions, so the items must be read separately
why: enumerate pairs each item with a running count, replacing range(len(a)) when both are needed.

q: What does this program print?
options: tac
tic toe
tic tac toe
0 tic 2 toe
why: enumerate pairs each name with a count starting at 0, and the if keeps only the pairs whose count is even: positions 0 and 2.

q: What does zip do with sequences of different lengths, and what changes with strict=True?
options: It stops at the shortest by default, and strict=True raises ValueError instead
It pads the short ones with None by default, and strict=True removes the padding
It raises ValueError by default, and strict=True makes it stop at the shortest
It stops at the longest by default, and strict=True stops at the shortest
why: zip stops at the shortest by default; strict=True raises ValueError when the lengths differ instead of truncating silently.

q: What does this program print?
code:
pairs = list(zip('abc', [1, 2]))
try:
    list(zip('abc', [1, 2], strict=True))
    status = 'ok'
except ValueError:
    status = 'ValueError'
print(len(pairs), status)
options: 3 ValueError
2 ok
2 ValueError
3 ok
why: The plain zip stops at the shorter list and gives two pairs, while the strict version sees the lengths differ and raises ValueError.

q: Which pairing of a loop-control tool with its effect is correct?
options: break leaves the loop, continue skips to the next pass
break skips to the next pass, continue leaves the loop
continue ends the whole program, break ends one pass
break and continue both restart the loop from the first item
why: break ends the loop at once while continue skips the rest of the block and goes on with the loop.

q: What is an early exit from a loop?
options: A loop whose body runs zero times
Leaving the loop, or the whole program, before the loop's own test would end it
Skipping one pass and carrying on with the next
A loop that stops because its sequence ran out of items
why: Some programs must leave a loop, or the whole program, before the loop's own test would.

q: When loops are nested, which loop does break end?
options: All the enclosing loops at once
The outermost loop
Only the loop that has an else clause
The innermost enclosing loop
why: break ends the innermost enclosing for or while loop at once.

q: What does this program print?
options: 0 0; end
why: break ends only the inner loop, so each pass of the outer loop prints one pair with b equal to 0 and then the outer loop goes on.

q: What does this program print?
options: else 2
else 1
why: break ends the loop at once and skips its else clause, and the loop variable keeps the value it had when the loop was left.

q: Which exception does sys.exit() raise?
options: KeyboardInterrupt
RuntimeError
ExitError
SystemExit
why: sys.exit() raises SystemExit, which ends the program unless something intercepts it.

q: What does this program print?
options: caught 3 after
after
caught 3
caught None after
why: sys.exit(3) only raises SystemExit, so an except clause can catch it, and the program goes on after the try statement; the exception carries the argument 3.

q: How does skipping a pass differ from leaving a loop?
options: Skipping ends the loop, leaving goes on with the next pass
Skipping goes on with the next pass, leaving ends the loop
Skipping ends the program, leaving ends only the loop
They are the same, only the keyword differs
why: Skipping a pass is different from leaving the loop: the loop continues.

q: In a while loop, where does execution go after continue?
options: Back to test the loop's condition
To the first line after the loop
To the next line of the block
Out of the loop, skipping its else clause
why: continue skips the rest of the block and goes back to test the condition of a while loop.

q: What does this program print?
why: continue skips the adding for 3 and 6, so the total is 1 + 2 + 4 + 5 + 7.

q: In a while loop, why is a continue placed before the line that changes the counter risky?
options: continue ends the loop, so the counter is never used
continue resets the counter to zero
It goes back to the test without changing the counter, so the condition may never change
Python forbids any statement after continue in a block
why: continue skips the rest of the block and goes back to test the condition, so lines after it do not run on that pass.

q: Which pair of facts about a finished loop over a non-empty sequence is true?
options: The else clause runs after every break, and the loop variable is deleted
The loop variable is deleted, and the else clause runs only after an exception
The else clause never runs, and the loop variable is reset to 0
The else clause shows that break was not used, and the loop variable keeps its last value
why: How a loop finishes can be told apart from how it was left, and the loop variable is not deleted when the loop ends.

q: Which task fits the else clause of a for loop best?
options: Run cleanup code even if an exception happens
Run the block a second time if the first pass failed
Report that a search went through everything and found nothing
Run when the loop's sequence is empty and only then
why: The else clause runs when the loop finishes without break, which is the tidy way to say searched everything and found nothing.

q: What does this program print?
options: no even
even 8
even 8 no even
even 3
why: The loop reaches 8, prints and breaks, so the else clause, which runs only when the loop ends without break, is skipped.

q: What does this program print?
options: found found missing
found missing found
found missing missing
missing missing missing
why: A return inside the loop skips the else clause, and a search that finds nothing, including one over an empty list, runs it.

q: After a for loop over a non-empty list ends, what does its loop variable hold?
options: Nothing, because the name is deleted when the loop ends
The value of the last pass, since the name is not deleted
The first item of the list
The number of passes the loop made
why: The loop variable is overwritten on each pass and is not deleted when the loop ends.

q: What does this program print?
why: The for statement overwrites its target on every pass, so changing i inside the block does not change the loop, and after the last pass i still holds what the block last gave it: 2 * 10.

q: What does this program print?
options: None
NameError
why: After a loop over an empty sequence the loop variable was never assigned, so using it raises NameError.

q: What must a program do before it can call a standard library function such as randint?
options: Nothing, all library functions are always available
Copy the function's code into the program
Save the program in the same folder as Python
Import the module that holds the function
why: A program reaches the standard library's functions by importing the module that holds them.

q: How many forms of the import statement does the chapter show?
options: Three: one module, several modules on one line, and a star import
One, since all imports work the same way
Two: import and export
Four, one for each kind of module
why: The chapter shows three forms of the import statement, and PEP 8 has a view on each.

q: After import random, how does a program call the function randint?
options: randint(1, 10), with no prefix
import.randint(1, 10)
random.randint(1, 10), with the module name in front
random(randint, 1, 10)
why: import makes a module's names available under the module's name, as random.randint(1, 10).

q: What does this program print?
options: NameError 2
NameError NameError
2 NameError
why: After a plain import the function is only available under the module's name, so floor alone is unknown, while math.floor(2.7) works.

q: What does import random, sys, os, math do, and what does PEP 8 usually say about it?
options: Imports only random, and PEP 8 prefers this form
Imports all four modules in one statement, and PEP 8 prefers separate lines
Imports all four, and PEP 8 requires this form
Raises SyntaxError, since one import can name only one module
why: One import statement can name several modules separated by commas, but PEP 8 says imports should usually be on separate lines.

q: What does this program print?
code:
import math, string
print(math.ceil(2.1), string.ascii_lowercase[:3])
options: 2 abc
3 a
2 cba
3 abc
why: Both modules are imported by one statement and stay under their own names: math.ceil(2.1) rounds up to 3 and the first three lowercase letters are abc.

q: Why do the chapter and PEP 8 discourage from random import *?
options: It hides which names are present, and the full name reads better
It is slower to run than a plain import
It imports only the first function of the module
It stops working when the module has more than ten names
why: The chapter concludes that the full name makes more readable code, and PEP 8 says wildcard imports make it unclear which names are present.

q: What does this program print?
code:
from math import *
print(sqrt(9), pi > 3)
options: 3 True
3.0 False
3.0 True
NameError
why: from math import * brings sqrt and pi in without the module prefix, so sqrt(9) is the float 3.0 and pi is above 3.

q: A file has two star imports and later calls sqrt(9). What is the reader's problem?
options: The second star import deletes the first one
Python raises an error for a second star import
The call runs twice, once for each module
They cannot tell which module the name sqrt came from
why: Wildcard imports make it unclear which names are present, so the origin of a bare name is hidden.

q: Why does an advanced course add a section beyond the chapter's loops?
options: Because the chapter's loops no longer work in current Python
To replace for and while by newer statements
To pair the loops with what current Python offers and the hazards the documentation names
To teach features that only exist in Python 3.14
why: An advanced course pairs the chapter's loops with what current Python offers for the same jobs, and with the hazards the reference documentation names.

q: Which two features does the expression style group cover?
options: The range function and the enumerate function
The break statement and the continue statement
Star imports and the sys.exit function
The := assignment expression in loop conditions and the PEP 8 advice on imports
why: Two recent language and style features shorten and tidy the loops and imports the chapter teaches.

q: Since which Python version can := name a value inside a condition?
why: Since Python 3.8 an assignment expression names a value inside a condition.

q: What does this program print?
code:
items = iter(['ab', 'cd', '', 'ef'])
got = []
while chunk := next(items):
    got.append(chunk)
print(got, repr(chunk))
options: ['ab', 'cd', 'ef'] 'ef'
['ab', 'cd'] 'cd'
why: The condition names each value as it tests it, so the loop stops at the empty string, which is false, and chunk still holds that value afterwards.

q: What does PEP 8 advise about wildcard imports?
options: Avoid them, with one exception for republishing an internal interface as a public API
Use them whenever a module has many names
Use them only inside functions
Always use them for the standard library
why: PEP 8 advises against wildcard imports, with the single defensible exception of republishing an internal interface as part of a public API.

q: A file needs os, sys and math. Which arrangement follows the PEP 8 advice?
options: One line: import os, sys, math
One line per module, each written as a star import
One star import from a module that holds all three
Three lines, one import statement per module, and no wildcard
why: PEP 8 advises one import per line and against wildcard imports.

q: What do the two hazards in this group have in common?
options: Both are errors that stop the program at once
Both only occur in old versions of Python
Both are caused by using range() the wrong way
Both are traps named in the reference documentation that are easy to write without noticing
why: Two hazards the documentation names are worth teaching beside the chapter's programs.

q: What is the tutorial's remedy for changing a collection while looping over it?
options: Loop over a copy, or build a new collection
Change the collection only inside a continue statement
Sort the collection before the loop
Use while True: so the loop never ends
why: Changing a collection while iterating over it is tricky to get right; the remedy is to loop over a copy or build a new collection.

q: What does this program print?
why: Removing items from the list being looped over shifts the later items so some are never visited, while looping over a copy visits them all.

q: What does this program print?
options: RuntimeError
KeyError
why: Deleting from the dictionary that the loop is walking over is the hazard the tutorial names, and Python stops the loop with an error.

q: What does Python 3.14 do when return, break or continue leaves a finally block?
options: It raises a SyntaxError and refuses to run the file
It says nothing, as in every earlier version
It raises RuntimeError when the statement is reached
The compiler emits a SyntaxWarning
why: Python 3.14 makes the compiler emit a SyntaxWarning when a return, break or continue statement has the effect of leaving a finally block, as PEP 765 specifies.

q: Under Python 3.14, a script has break inside a finally block in a loop. What happens when it is run?
options: The script does not start at all because of a SyntaxError
The compiler warns, and the script still runs
Nothing at all is reported
The break is silently turned into a continue
why: The change adds a SyntaxWarning, which is a warning and not an error, so the code is still compiled and run.
